text: Verify the build that actually exists
After this you can compare installed hardware and software with accepted build records.

A physical audit compares the actual item with the detailed description that applies to its version. A reviewer may examine labels, parts, assembly records, software versions, deviations and change history. It is a correspondence check, not simply a count of parts. When a unit differs, establish whether a valid change or approved exception explains it; otherwise record the mismatch.

items: Confirm the serial number, product revision and relevant build record. You should see: The unit and the expected description are unambiguous. If not: Resolve identity discrepancies before comparing details.
Inspect a representative set of controlled features. You should see: Markings, versions and components can be matched. If not: Expand the inspection when unexplained differences appear.
Compare changes and approved exceptions. You should see: Allowed departures are distinguished from unknown ones. If not: Require the actual approval evidence.
Document differences and closure evidence. You should see: A reviewer can see the final disposition. If not: Keep unsupported claims open.
A controller can bear the correct housing label but contain a different assembly revision. Checking both identifies a mismatch a label-only review would miss.

text: Compare the actual unit with the version explicitly applicable to it.
A physical inspection alone does not establish all functional performance.

items: Assuming a matching model name proves full conformity Products with one name may have different internal revisions. Fix: Check selected critical identifiers and records.
